chapters.title: Chapter 6: Financing Working Capital in India

lessons.title: Cash Credit, Overdraft, WCDL and Commercial Paper Compared

children.text: Once you know how much working capital you need and how much your bank will lend, one decision remains: which instrument to use. Most Indian businesses answer this by default, putting everything on the cash credit limit because that is what was sanctioned first.
That default costs money. The instruments differ in price, in flexibility, in what they are secured against and in what happens when you cannot repay. This lesson sets them side by side.
The Instruments

cells: Cash credit
Revolving limit, drawn and repaid freely, interest on the daily balance
Hypothecation of stock and book debts
Highest of the bank options
Highest: draw exactly what you need, when you need it
Overdraft
Limit on the current account, usually not linked to stock
Property, deposits or other collateral
Similar to cash credit, sometimes higher
High, but the limit is not stock-driven so it does not flex with the cycle
Working capital demand loan
Fixed amount for a fixed tenor, from seven days upward, repaid at maturity
Same charge as the cash credit limit it is carved from
Usually a little below cash credit
Low: the amount is fixed for the tenor
Bill discounting
The bank pays you now against an accepted invoice or bill and collects from the buyer later
The bill itself, strongest when backed by a letter of credit
Low when the buyer is strong or the bill is LC-backed
Transaction by transaction
Commercial paper
Unsecured money market instrument issued at a discount to face value
None, so it rests entirely on the credit rating
Lowest, for well-rated issuers
Low: issued in tranches, with refinancing risk at maturity

children.text: Two of these deserve a closer look, because they are where most of the saving sits.
A
working capital demand loan
is usually carved out of the same sanctioned limit as the
cash credit

facility. You commit to a fixed amount for a fixed period and pay a slightly lower rate for that certainty. The trade-off is real: if your cash position improves mid-tenor, you cannot repay it early the way you can sweep a cash credit account.

markDefs.definition: Working capital demand loan. A fixed amount drawn for a fixed tenor within the same sanctioned limit, repaid in full at maturity.
Cash credit. A revolving limit secured by hypothecation of stock and book debts, where interest is charged only on the daily outstanding balance.

children.text: Commercial paper

is a different world. It is unsecured, issued directly to investors rather than borrowed from a bank, and priced off the money market rather than off your banking relationship. Under the Reserve Bank's 2024 directions, the tenor runs from seven days to one year, the minimum denomination is ₹5 lakh and multiples of that, and the issuer needs a credit rating of at least A3 from a registered rating agency.

markDefs.definition: Commercial paper. An unsecured short-term money market instrument issued at a discount to face value by rated companies.

body.caption: Commercial paper is issued at a discount: you receive the proceeds now and repay the full face value at maturity

children.text: On a ₹30 crore, 90-day issue at a yield of 7.35%, the proceeds are about ₹29.466 crore and you repay ₹30 crore at maturity, a discount of roughly ₹0.53 crore. Add rating fees, issuing and paying agent charges and stamp duty, and the all-in cost lands near 7.6%, still well below any bank line.
What the Choice Is Worth

Take a business needing ₹50 crore of working capital funding through the year. Assume cash credit at 9.5%, a demand loan at 9% and commercial paper all-in at 7.6%. These are illustrative rates, and your own will depend on your rating, your relationship and the market.

body.title: Annual funding cost under three structures (₹ crore)

stats.label: Demand loan blend
stats.context: Saves ₹17 lakh by fixing the permanent portion

stats.label: Commercial paper blend
stats.context: Saves ₹57 lakh, but only for rated issuers who can refinance

body.text: Notice how the structure mirrors Chapter 3. The permanent layer of working capital suits a demand loan or commercial paper, both of which are cheaper and both of which need repaying on a date. The fluctuating layer belongs on cash credit, where you pay for flexibility and use it. Paying cash credit rates on a permanent need is buying flexibility you never exercise.

body.title: Price the switch
body.prompt: A company currently funds ₹20 crore permanently on its cash credit limit at 9.5%. Its bank offers to convert that portion into a working capital demand loan at 8.9%. How much does the company save in a year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: The saving is the rate difference of 0.6 percentage points applied to ₹20 crore, which is ₹0.12 crore, or about ₹12 lakh a year. The cost is flexibility: that ₹20 crore is now committed for the tenor, so the switch only makes sense for the portion of the need that genuinely never goes away.

children.text: The Risk Nobody Prices Until It Bites
Cheaper instruments carry
rollover risk

. Commercial paper matures on a date and has to be refinanced by issuing fresh paper. In normal markets that is routine. When money market conditions tighten, or when your own rating comes under pressure, the paper does not roll, and the entire amount falls due at once.

markDefs.definition: The risk that a short-term instrument cannot be refinanced at maturity, or can only be refinanced at a much higher cost.

body.text: This is exactly how several Indian non-bank finance companies ran into trouble in 2018 and 2019: short-term paper funding longer-term assets, refinanced repeatedly until one day it could not be. The lesson generalises beyond finance companies. Any business funding a permanent need with instruments that mature every 90 days is exposed to a market it does not control.

children.text: The defence is a committed backup line. Keep enough undrawn bank limit to repay a maturing tranche without refinancing, and treat that undrawn portion as the price of using cheap money, not as spare capacity.

body.title: Bank lines against money market funding

columns.label: Bank facilities
points: Relationship-priced, so they move slowly and predictably
Secured, which means margins and drawing power constrain access
Renewable annually, with the limit reviewed rather than repaid
Available to businesses of any size and rating
More expensive, and the cost of the relationship is embedded in the rate

columns.label: Commercial paper and money market instruments
points: Market-priced, so the cost moves with liquidity conditions
Unsecured, resting entirely on the credit rating
Must be repaid in full at maturity and reissued
Available only to rated issuers of reasonable size
Cheaper, with the saving effectively paying you to carry refinancing risk

body.title: Trade finance: the instruments most exporters and importers underuse

children.text: Exporters have access to concessional finance that ordinary working capital borrowers do not.
Packing credit

, also called pre-shipment credit, is advanced against a confirmed export order to fund production, and is typically priced below a normal cash credit line. It can be taken in rupees or in foreign currency, where it is priced off an international benchmark and also hedges the currency exposure naturally, since the loan is repaid out of the export proceeds.

markDefs.definition: Pre-shipment export credit, advanced against a confirmed export order to fund the production of the goods.

children.text: After shipment, post-shipment credit takes over: the export bill is discounted or negotiated, converting the receivable into cash immediately rather than waiting for the overseas buyer. Export credit insurance can cover the buyer default risk on top.

Importers have the mirror image. A letter of credit lets the supplier ship against bank undertaking rather than against your credit, and buyer's credit arranged through an overseas bank can fund the import for up to a year, often at a lower rate than domestic borrowing once hedging costs are counted. The hedging qualifier matters: an unhedged foreign currency borrowing looks cheap until the rupee moves, and businesses with no natural foreign currency earnings should treat that gap as a real cost rather than an optional one.

body.title: Which instrument fits the need?
body.question: A rated mid-cap manufacturer has ₹60 crore of working capital need, of which about ₹45 crore is present in every month of the year. It has an unused cash credit limit and wants to cut funding cost without taking undue risk. What is the most sensible structure?
options: Move the entire ₹60 crore to commercial paper, since it is the cheapest instrument
Fund the ₹45 crore permanent portion through a demand loan or commercial paper, keep the fluctuating ₹15 crore on cash credit, and retain undrawn limit as backup
Keep everything on cash credit, since flexibility is always worth paying for
Move the fluctuating ₹15 crore to commercial paper and keep the permanent ₹45 crore on cash credit
body.explanation: Match the instrument to the layer. The permanent portion suits fixed-tenor funding, which is cheaper, while the fluctuating portion needs the flexibility of cash credit. Funding everything through commercial paper concentrates refinancing risk, and the last option is backwards: it puts the volatile need on the instrument that cannot flex.

body.title: The instrument that must be repaid
body.textWithBlank: Unlike a cash credit limit, which is renewed annually, a working capital ___ loan is drawn for a fixed tenor and must be repaid in full at maturity, which is why it prices slightly lower.
body.explanation: A working capital demand loan gives the bank certainty of repayment on a date, and the borrower is compensated with a lower rate. The cost is flexibility, so it suits the permanent layer of working capital.

body.title: Cheap money with a date attached
body.scenario: A chemicals company with an A1 short-term rating funds ₹80 crore of working capital, of which ₹60 crore is permanent. Its treasurer proposes replacing ₹60 crore of cash credit at 9.4% with rolling 90-day commercial paper at an all-in cost of about 7.5%, saving roughly ₹1.1 crore a year. The cash credit limit would be reduced to ₹20 crore to save on unused limit charges, and the company has no other committed lines.
body.prompt: Would you approve this? What would you change?
body.modelAnswer:
Approve the idea, reject the structure.

The saving is real: 1.9 percentage points on ₹60 crore is about ₹1.14 crore a year, and a well-rated issuer funding a permanent need at money market rates is doing the right thing in principle.

The problem is the last sentence. Cutting the cash credit limit to ₹20 crore leaves no capacity to repay a ₹60 crore tranche that fails to roll. Commercial paper matures every 90 days, and the company would be betting four times a year that the market is open and its rating is intact. The one time that bet fails, the company has to find ₹60 crore in days, with no committed line behind it.

What to change. Keep a committed backup facility sized to cover at least the largest single maturing tranche, which means retaining most of the existing limit even though some of it sits unused. Pay the commitment charge and treat it as the insurance premium on the saving. Stagger the issuance so tranches mature at different dates rather than all at once, which turns a cliff into a series of steps. And set a rule in advance for what happens if paper prices above a defined spread: at that point you draw on the bank line rather than issuing at any cost, because a rating under pressure is exactly when the market prices you worst.

Net effect: instead of saving ₹1.14 crore with a tail risk nobody has priced, the company saves perhaps ₹0.9 crore with the risk covered. That is a better trade, and it is one the board can actually approve.

body.label: The rule that survives every cycle
body.value: Cheap short-term money needs a committed backup line
body.context: The saving from money market funding is real, and so is the obligation to repay on a date. Undrawn bank limit is not idle capacity, it is the insurance that makes the cheaper instrument safe to use.

cards.definition: Revolving limit against stock and book debts, interest on the daily balance, repayable on demand. Most flexible, most expensive.
Current account limit, usually secured against property or deposits rather than stock, so it does not flex with the operating cycle.
Fixed amount, fixed tenor from seven days upward, carved from the same limit and priced slightly lower.
Cash today against an accepted bill, cheapest when backed by a letter of credit.
Unsecured discount instrument, seven days to one year, minimum ₹5 lakh denomination, minimum A3 rating.
Pre-shipment export finance against a confirmed order, typically at concessional rates.
Overseas funding for an import, cheap before hedging and not necessarily cheap after it.

body.title: Review your funding mix once a year
steps: Split the requirement into the permanent layer and the fluctuating layer, using the method from Chapter 3.
Price each layer against the instruments actually available to you, not the theoretical list.
Ask your bank what the demand loan rate would be against your current cash credit rate, since the gap is negotiable.
If you are rated and large enough, get a commercial paper programme priced, even if you do not use it immediately.
For every rupee of money market funding, confirm how it would be repaid if the paper failed to roll.
Keep committed undrawn bank limit at least equal to the largest single maturing tranche.
If you export, check whether pre-shipment and post-shipment credit are being used to their full eligibility.
For foreign currency borrowing, cost it after hedging unless you have natural foreign currency earnings.

body.text: Every step down in funding cost is a step up in the obligation to repay on a fixed date. The saving is the price the market pays you for taking refinancing risk, so make sure you have actually decided to take it.

points: Cash credit is the most flexible and most expensive option, with interest charged on the daily outstanding balance.
A working capital demand loan is carved from the same limit at a slightly lower rate, in exchange for a fixed amount and a fixed tenor.
Commercial paper is unsecured money market funding for rated issuers, with a tenor of seven days to one year, minimum denomination of ₹5 lakh and a minimum A3 rating.
Match instruments to layers: fixed-tenor funding for the permanent portion, cash credit for the fluctuating portion.
In the worked example, blending instruments cut the annual funding cost by ₹17 lakh to ₹57 lakh on a ₹50 crore requirement.
Cheaper short-term instruments carry rollover risk, which needs a committed backup line rather than optimism.
Exporters and importers have access to packing credit, post-shipment credit, letters of credit and buyer's credit, which are frequently underused.
